The manipulation of time in the story is exceptionally well-balanced and serves the emotional weight of the narrative. In terms of "story time," the scene takes place over just a few minutes on a single afternoon. The author slightly stretches these brief moments by weaving in rich sensory details (the smell of diesel and cold coffee, the rattling of the suitcase wheels, the fine cracks on the pump hose) and physical pauses between lines of sparse dialogue. This slow, deliberate pacing mirrors the heavy, unhurried flow of the Elbe river and amplifies the unspoken tension between mother and son. 

At the same time, the author uses extreme compression to deliver the backstory. Years of Jonas's childhood, the implied death of Henning, and the long period of estrangement are condensed into single, evocative sentences (e.g., "Früher hatte er am Anleger gesessen...", "Henning hätte ihn im Frühjahr getauscht"). This contrast between the stretched, tense present and the compressed history makes the scene feel grounded, poignant, and deeply atmospheric.
